title: Equity securities and corporate actions: the Series 7 calculations

reading.h: Cumulative voting: same total, different spread
reading.body:
Under **both** statutory and cumulative voting, your **total votes = shares owned × seats up for election**. The method never changes that total. The exam's favorite trick asks "how many votes total?" Both methods give the same answer.

What differs is how you may spread the votes. **Statutory** voting caps you at your share count per candidate. **Cumulative** voting lets you pile every vote onto one candidate. That is why it helps small holders who want to win a single board seat.

Worked example. You own 300 shares and 4 directors are up for election. Total votes = 300 × 4 = **1,200** either way. Under statutory voting, the most you can give one candidate is 300 votes. Under cumulative voting, you can put all **1,200** votes on one candidate. When a stem asks for the maximum votes for one director, the method decides the answer.

reading.h: Dividends in arrears: don't forget the current year
reading.body:
Cumulative preferred piles up every skipped dividend as **dividends in arrears**. The company must pay all of them, **plus the current year**, before it pays any common dividend.

Formula: **Arrears owed = (years missed × annual dividend) + current-year dividend.**

Worked example. A **6% $100-par** cumulative preferred skips two years. The board now wants to pay a common dividend. Each preferred share must first get $6 + $6 for the two missed years + $6 for this year = **$18**.

Contrast a **straight** (non-cumulative) preferred with the same facts. It gets only the **current** $6. The missed years are gone for good. The classic trap answer leaves off the current year, so it shows $12 instead of $18.

reading.h: Convertible preferred: parity in both directions
reading.body:
Think of a convertible as a coupon for a fixed number of common shares.

**Conversion ratio (CR) = par ÷ conversion price.** A $100-par preferred convertible at $20 gives CR = 5 shares.

**Parity price of common = preferred price ÷ CR.** Preferred at $110 gives $110 ÷ 5 = **$22**. If the common trades above $22, you profit by converting.

**Parity price of preferred = common price × CR.** Common at $12 with CR 2 gives preferred parity of $24.

**Forced conversion** happens when the issuer calls a convertible. Compare all your exits. Take a $100-par 6% preferred convertible at $20, so CR is 5, callable at $103. The issuer calls it. The preferred trades at $104 and the common at $21.50. Converting gives 5 × $21.50 = **$107.50**. That beats the $104 market price and the $103 call, so "convert and sell" wins.

**Anti-dilution:** on a split or stock dividend, the CR is multiplied and the conversion price divided by the same factor. So the conversion value holds. The coupon still buys the same slice of the company.

A right's value depends on whether the stock still trades **with** the right attached.

**Cum-rights (before the ex-date): value = (Market − Subscription) ÷ (rights needed per new share + 1).**

**Ex-rights (on or after the ex-date): value = (Market − Subscription) ÷ (rights needed per new share).**

Memory: **cum** means "with," so add the 1 for the right inside the share itself. **Ex** means "without," so no 1.

Worked example. Stock $44, subscription $36, 3 rights needed per new share. **Cum-rights = ($44 − $36) ÷ (3 + 1) = $2.00.** Leave off the +1 and you get $2.67. That is the ex-rights value, and it is the trap when the stem says "before the ex-rights date." The two values stay in line because on the ex-date the stock price drops by exactly one right's value. **Warrants** are different. They are long-term sweeteners priced above market at issue with no intrinsic value. Never mix the two formulas.

reading.h: Splits, stock dividends, cost basis, and option adjustments
reading.body:
A split or stock dividend never changes total basis. It changes only the **per-share** basis. **Factor = split numerator ÷ denominator, or (1 + stock-dividend %).** New shares = old shares × factor. **New basis per share = old basis ÷ factor.** None of this is taxable, and the holding period carries over.

Worked. 200 shares at $60 basis, 20% stock dividend gives 240 shares. Basis = $12,000 ÷ 240 = **$50 per share**. The trap ($60 × 0.8 = $48) uses the wrong operation.

Listed options adjust the same way. An **even split (ends in :1)** multiplies the number of contracts by the factor, divides the strike by the factor, and keeps 100 shares. One Jan 200 call at 2:1 becomes two Jan 100 calls. An **uneven split, stock dividend, or reverse split** keeps the contracts the same, divides the strike by the factor, and sets the deliverable at 100 × factor shares. One Sep 90 put at 3:2 becomes one Sep 60 put on 150 shares. An ordinary cash dividend brings no option adjustment.

reading.h: Dividend dates under T+1, due bills, and the 25% rule
reading.body:
Since **2024-05-28** (T+1 settlement, FINRA Rule 11140 as amended), a **regular** cash dividend has its **ex-date equal to the record date**, as long as the record date is a business day. Here is why. A buyer must be settled by the record date. Settlement takes one business day. So a purchase on the record date settles one day too late. **The last day to buy and still get the dividend is the business day before the record date.** The old "one or two days before the record date" rules are out of date. Do not use them.

Worked. Record date Thursday March 12, no holidays, so the ex-date is **Thursday March 12**. The last day to buy for the dividend is Wednesday March 11.

**Large distributions (25% of value or more)**, such as big stock dividends and splits, work differently. The ex-date is the **first business day after the payable date**. Trades between the record and payable dates carry **due bills**. Worked: 30% stock dividend, record June 10, payable June 24, so the ex-date is **June 25**.

Rule 144 covers two groups. **Restricted stock** is bought unregistered from the issuer, such as in a private placement. **Control stock** is any stock owned by an **affiliate** (an officer, director, or 10%-or-more holder), even stock bought on the exchange. The rule of thumb: the holding period cures "unregistered," and the volume limit tames "insider." The **6-month** holding period for a reporting issuer applies only to restricted stock. Control stock bought in the open market has **no** holding period, but it still has a volume limit.

**Affiliate volume limit (any 3 months) = the GREATER of 1% of outstanding shares or the average weekly volume of the prior 4 weeks.** A **Form 144** is required when a sale tops **5,000 shares or $50,000** in 3 months.

Worked. 12,000,000 shares outstanding, so 1% = 120,000 shares. The prior 4 weeks' volume was 150,000, 130,000, 140,000, and 140,000 shares, an average of 140,000 shares. The maximum is the greater of 120,000 or 140,000, so **140,000 shares**.

**Spin-off** basis: split the original cost between the parent and the spun-off shares by relative fair market value. 100 shares, $5,000 basis. After the spin-off, the parent is worth $80 and the spinco $20 per original share. So 80% ($4,000) goes to the parent and 20% ($1,000) goes to the spinco. Holding periods carry over.

flashcards.front: Cumulative voting: total votes and max on one candidate
flashcards.back: Total = shares × seats, the same under both methods. Cumulative lets you put ALL votes on one candidate. Statutory caps you at your share count per candidate.

flashcards.front: Dividends in arrears owed before common
flashcards.back: (years missed × annual dividend) + current-year dividend. Straight preferred gets only the current year.
CR = par ÷ conversion price. ($100 par, $20 conv. price → 5 shares.)
Work out CR × common price, the value of the shares now. Compare it to the market price and the call price. Pick the largest, usually 'convert and sell.'
Cum: (Market − Subscription) ÷ (rights needed + 1). Ex: (Market − Subscription) ÷ (rights needed). Cum = 'with' → +1.

flashcards.front: Per-share basis after a split/stock dividend
flashcards.back: New basis = old basis ÷ factor. Factor = split ratio or (1 + stock-dividend %). Total basis and holding period do not change. Not taxable.

flashcards.front: Option adjustment: even vs. uneven split
flashcards.back: Even (ends in :1): contracts × factor, strike ÷ factor, still 100 shares. Uneven/stock dividend/reverse: contracts unchanged, strike ÷ factor, deliverable = 100 × factor.
Regular dividend: ex-date = record date (last day to buy = business day before record). Distributions ≥ 25%: ex-date = first business day AFTER payable; due bills between record and payable.
Greater of 1% of outstanding shares OR average weekly volume of the prior 4 weeks. Form 144 required if sale > 5,000 shares or > $50,000 in 3 months.
Split the original basis between parent and spinco by relative fair market value. Holding period carries over.

quiz.stem: A 5% $100-par cumulative preferred stock has paid no dividends for the past two years. Before the company can pay any dividend on its common stock this year, each preferred share must receive:
quiz.explanation: Cumulative preferred must clear all arrears plus the current year: $5 + $5 (two skipped years) + $5 (current) = $15. Forgetting the current year gives the $10 trap; $20 assumes three missed years.

quiz.stem: A shareholder owns 300 shares of a company that uses cumulative voting. Four directors are being elected. The maximum number of votes the shareholder may cast for a single candidate is:
quiz.explanation: Total votes = shares × seats = 300 × 4 = 1,200, and cumulative voting lets the holder pile all 1,200 on one candidate. 300 is the statutory-voting maximum per candidate (the trap), and 75 wrongly divides rather than multiplies.

quiz.stem: A $100-par convertible preferred stock is convertible into common at $20 per share and currently trades at $110. The parity price of the common stock is:
quiz.explanation: CR = par ÷ conversion price = $100 ÷ $20 = 5 shares; parity of common = preferred price ÷ CR = $110 ÷ 5 = $22. Using the conversion price itself ($20) ignores the preferred's premium over par; $550 multiplies instead of divides.

quiz.stem: XYZ common trades at $44. The company offers existing shareholders new shares at $36, with 3 rights required to buy one new share. Before the ex-rights date, the theoretical value of one right is:
quiz.explanation: Cum-rights (before the ex-date) = (Market − Subscription) ÷ (rights needed + 1) = ($44 − $36) ÷ (3 + 1) = $2.00. Omitting the +1 gives $2.67, which is the ex-rights value and the classic trap when the stem says 'before the ex-rights date.'

quiz.stem: An officer of a company with 12,000,000 common shares outstanding files Form 144 to sell control stock. Trading volume over the four preceding weeks was 150,000, 130,000, 140,000 and 140,000 shares. The maximum shares she may sell under Rule 144 in the next three months is:
quiz.explanation: Rule 144(e) permits the GREATER of 1% of outstanding shares (120,000) or the average weekly volume of the prior four weeks (560,000 ÷ 4 = 140,000), so 140,000. 120,000 uses only the 1% test, 150,000 grabs the single highest week, and 560,000 forgets to average.

quiz.stem: An investor owns 200 shares of XYZ purchased at $60 per share. XYZ distributes a 20% stock dividend. After the distribution, the investor's cost basis per share is:
quiz.explanation: Total basis stays $12,000; shares rise to 200 × 1.20 = 240, so per-share basis = $12,000 ÷ 240 = $50. Multiplying $60 by 0.8 ($48) applies the wrong operation, and the basis is never left unchanged at $60 after more shares are added.

quiz.stem: A $100-par 6% preferred stock is convertible at $20 and callable at $103. The company announces it will call the entire issue. The preferred trades at $104 and the common at $21.50. Which action produces the greatest value for a holder?
options: Accept the call and receive $103 per share
Sell the preferred in the market at $104
Convert to common and sell the common shares
Hold the preferred and keep collecting the 6% dividend
quiz.explanation: CR = $100 ÷ $20 = 5 shares, so converting yields 5 × $21.50 = $107.50 — more than the $104 market price or the $103 call. Holding is not viable once the issue is called (the dividend stops), so 'convert and sell' wins.

quiz.stem: A corporation declares a 30% stock dividend with a record date of Wednesday, June 10, and a payable date of Wednesday, June 24 (all business days). The ex-dividend date is:
quiz.explanation: For distributions of 25% or more, FINRA Rule 11140(b)(2) sets the ex-date as the first business day AFTER the payable date — June 25 — with due bills covering trades between record and payable. The record-date answer (June 10) is correct only for regular distributions under T+1, not large ones.
